questions.q: Why does an untracked asset receive none of the protections covered earlier in this chapter, such as EDR or patch management?
options: Because those programs only act on assets listed in an inventory or CMDB, and can't protect what they don't know exists
Because EDR agents automatically install themselves on every device within range
Because untracked assets are physically disconnected from the network by default
Because signature-based antivirus works without needing to know a device exists
questions.explain: IT can't push an EDR agent, patch a server, or review logs for a device it has no record of. An untracked asset is pure attack surface with zero defenses applied to it.

options: A Configuration Management Database — a system of record tracking known assets, their owner, OS, patch level, and criticality
A type of commercial EDR agent
A Linux kernel audit framework
A firewall rule set
questions.explain: The CMDB is the system of record that patch management, vulnerability scanning, and EDR deployment all draw their scope from.

questions.q: What does a network discovery scan do?
options: Actively sweeps a network range to find devices that are actually alive and responding right now
Reads the CMDB and trusts its contents without verification
Only scans devices that already have an EDR agent installed
Deletes any device it finds that isn't in the CMDB
questions.explain: A tool like nmap -sn pings every address in a subnet to find what's actually present on the network, independent of what any inventory records.

questions.q: What does "shadow IT" refer to in this context?
options: Assets that are live on the network but aren't tracked in the CMDB or asset inventory
Any device running an operating system other than Windows
A type of malware that hides its own process tree
The portion of a CMDB reserved for retired assets
questions.explain: Shadow IT is exactly the gap a discovery scan reveals: real, running devices the CMDB has no record of.

questions.q: In the lesson's example, what made the forgotten test VM a real risk two years later?
options: It kept running an unpatched, vulnerable version of SQL Server, reachable on the internal network, with no EDR agent because it was never tracked
It had been encrypted by ransomware the day it was created
It was physically removed from the building but still powered on
It had a CMDB entry that was simply marked as low priority
questions.explain: Because the VM was never entered into the CMDB, it received no patches and no EDR coverage, leaving a well-known, years-old vulnerability exposed the entire time.
